Combined regime: parent national framework (US-like 2025-2026 executive orders on passports, entry screening, facilities in some states, immigration custody abuses, conversion-therapy-like prison policies) plus a highly protective division (Massachusetts-like: public accommodations protections, shield law, self-ID documents, hate crimes, "Most Protective" tier).

Rule 12/combined-regime override: rate the combined operative regime. National passport/entry rules apply regardless of division protections. A visitor's passport is issued nationally — the division cannot change the visitor's passport marker. Entry screening cable: discrepancy in documents → refuse, possible fraud finding. Trans travelers report passports confiscated/blocked abroad (that's issuance, affecting residents mostly, but for a visitor from abroad the foreign passport isn't affected — wait, the parent framework is the country's own passport regime; a foreign trans visitor carries their home passport. Hmm. But the parent's entry screening applies: officers told to refuse where discrepancy or doubt about sex, considering fraud/lifetime ineligibility for misrepresentation. That's directly visitor-facing — universal-exposure at the border. Also body scanner/outing at airport security (axis A).

Facilities: division has no ban and public accommodation protections covering GI — operative protection for hotels, restaurants, shops, transport. But national facilities bans apply to federal buildings (10 units all-government bans + others at least some gov buildings — presumably federal buildings too? The map is state/province bans; the national EO bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities). A visitor could enter federal buildings/post offices — national rule bars congruent-facility use in federally funded single-sex facilities. That's a universal-exposure measure, tier 1, though limited to government settings.

Immigration custody abuse (trans men forced labor, beatings, sexual abuse) — tier 1/2 state-tolerated targeting in immigration detention. A visitor faces immigration processes; detention risk if entry denied? Detention for visa overstay etc. Documented abuse of trans immigrants in custody is severe.

Sodomy law on books unenforceable since 1974 — secondary, tangential, per rule 2, must not dominate.

Violence: hate crime statute covering GI, hate-crime reporting unit, functional. No documented trans killings in dossier. National: 66% support birth-sex markers — social climate conservative-leaning nationally, but division is protective (67.8% ballot retention of public accommodations).

Overall: what happens if outed? At the border: potential secondary screening, refusal under the cable, possible fraud finding — but "never automatic," four elements, waiver. Street level in the division: protected public accommodations, hate crime law, functioning remedies. National facilities: exclusion from federal single-sex facilities. Immigration custody: severe but only if detained — probability low-ish for a lawful visitor but nonzero.

Score derivation: Exposures are mostly tier 1-ish (national entry screening, federal facility exclusion) but the entry refusal is not imprisonment; immigration custody abuse is severe (tier 2 documented state-tolerated targeting) though contingent on detention. Division protections are strong and operative (documented popular vote, enforcement machinery).

Compare anchors: 0.55-B (border secondary screening, discretionary refusal, administrative penalties, slow remedies) — quite similar for the entry axis. 0.65 anchors — documented protections working plus friction. 0.75-C — border training on respectful inspection... less so here.

Worst documented feature: national entry cable with possible lifetime ineligibility fraud finding + documented immigration custody abuse of trans detainees (beatings, sexual abuse, forced labor) = state-tolerated targeting (tier 2) for those in custody. Also national facility exclusion (tier 1, partial — federally funded single-sex facilities). Plus state-level facility bans don't apply in this division but do in others — the visitor is in this division; combined regime includes state laws of the division visited. Federal buildings in the division: national EO bars trans from gov-funded single-sex facilities.

Frequency: custody abuse requires detention — low probability for a tourist but severe. Entry screening friction is universal-ish (documents, scanners).

I'd put this around 0.60-0.65. Division is "Most Protective," public accommodations operative, hate-crime functioning, shield law. National layer adds meaningful exposure: border discretion with fraud-finding risk, federal facility exclusion, hostile national climate, possible detention abuse. Rule 11: functioning courts — national courts have enjoined several orders, ACLU suing; partial recourse operating.

Let's say 0.62. Or 0.65? The national entry regime is a genuine universal exposure (document examination → doubt about sex → refusal; possible fraud finding), plus custody tier-2 severity. Anchor 0.35-A: border bar for trans visitors, routine denial, no remedy — here refusal is discretionary, requires discrepancy, waivers exist, and courts are actively reviewing; less severe than Vellandra. Anchor 0.55-B: secondary screening, discretionary refusal under public order grounds, slow remedies — quite close to the entry axis, but the division's street-level protections are much stronger than 0.55's. Anchor 0.65-A: brief detention, complaint with apology/compensation, broadly safe capital — fits division street level well, but national custody abuse is worse than anything in 0.65 anchors. 0.75-C: trained border officers, low-moderate severity — national cable contradicts trained/respectful framing.

Balance: strongest protections concentrated and operative locally; exposures at national border/federal/custody stages. 0.62 feels right — above 0.55 because local protections are documented-operative and entry consequences are administrative-with-remedy, below 0.75 because national universal exposures (facility exclusion, entry refusal/fraud risk) and documented custody abuse of trans detainees.

I'll go 0.62.
